senses: A person who studies or collects folklore
The perception of or belief in connectedness among unrelated phenomena.
ety: From German Apophänie, from Ancient Greek ἀποφαίνω (apophaínō, “to appear”), from ἀπο- (apo-) and φαίνω (phaínō, “appear”), coined by German psychiatrist Klaus Conrad in 1958.

senses: An insistence on pure or unmixed forms.
An insistence on the traditionally correct way of doing things.
ety: From French purisme. By surface analysis, pur(e) + -ism.

senses: A situation involving a great deal of rhyming.
examples: Take heed when the Counsil take Chuck D's 1996 "No" and deliver a rhymefest called "Yes" — it's a sure sign that four talented volcanoes are about to erupt.

senses: Any item with four arms or four feet, such as a light stand, a gun mount, etc.
A concrete structure with arms, used to arrest wave energy along the shore in sea defence projects.
Any vertebrate with four limbs.
Any member of the superclass Tetrapoda
Any vertebrate (such as birds or snakes) that has evolved from early tetrapods
Synonym of rough breathing.
ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek δασεῖα (daseîa).

senses: Within the stomach.
a Betamax (videocassette tape)
coagulated chicken blood that is boiled, cut in to cubes, skewered and grilled to be sold as a street food
ety: Genericized trademark from Betamax. The food is named from their resemblance to the cuboidal videocassettes.

senses: A doctrine that universals do not have an existence except as names for classes of concrete objects.
ety: From French nominalisme. By surface analysis, nominal + -ism.

senses: A form of fossilization in which the organic parts of an organism are replaced by minerals.
The breakdown of organic matter in the soil to form soluble inorganic compounds.
One who trips or stumbles.
A person experiencing a hallucinogenic trip.
Synonym of tripman.
A member of the first generation of Japanese immigrants to North America, South America, or Australia.
Beaming, shining (especially with reference to a person's face or eyes).
ety: From a- + beam (“to emit beams of light”).

senses: One who, or that which, stifles; one who represses or limits.
A close-quarter combat weapon with the main fighting part of the weapon placed on the end of a long shaft, typically of wood.
ety: From pole + arm. The term is of modern provenance, not appearing until the late 1800s.

senses: A subspecies of plum tree, Prunus domestica subsp. insititia, native to Eurasia.
The edible fruit of this tree.
ety: From Middle English damascene, damasyn, damacene, from Latin prūnum damascēnum (“Damascene plum, plum of Damascus”). Doublet of damascene.

senses: One who is uncareful or unconcerned about appearance or surroundings, usually said of a dirty and untidy woman.
ety: Dating from the 17th century; related to slattering (“slovenly”), from the dialectal verb slatter (“to slop, to spill”).

senses: Someone or something that blows a horn.
ety: From horn + blower, or from Old English hornblāwere.

senses: One who studies paleontology.
examples: In the late nineteenth century, paleontologists began to catalog the many curious correspondences exhibited by fossils gathered on different continents.

senses: Devoted to, or inclined to attach great importance to, the order and ritual of a particular section of the Christian church.
In accordance with ecclesiastical standards or ceremonies; appropriate for or befitting a church.
Characteristic of a church; churchy.
ety: From Middle English *chirchely, *chirchelich, from Old English ċiriclīċ (“ecclesiastical”), equivalent to church + -ly. Cognate with Scots kirkly (“ecclesiastical”), Dutch kerkelijk (“ecclesiastic, ecclesiastical”), German kirchlich (“ecclesiastical, religious, ecclesiastic”), Swedish kyrklig (“ecclesiastical”). Compare also churchlike.

senses: An organic fungicide and insecticide sprayed on cereal grasses, fruit trees, etc.
ety: From “zinc ethylene bisdithiocarbamate”, its chemical name.

senses: Supervening; occurring subsequently; coming after something, especially when not causally connected.
ety: From Latin supervenient-, stem of superveniens, present participle of supervenio (“to come to or in addition to, to overtake”).

senses: A kind of path for use by cyclists and pedestrians in Milton Keynes, Buckinghamshire, England, generally surfaced with red tarmac.
Not avenged.
A geographic and/or institutional grouping of five cities
A person who keeps an aquarium.
One who kemps, or strives, for superiority; a champion or knight-errant.
ety: From kemp (“to contend, struggle, compete”) + -er. Compare Middle Low German kemper, Dutch kamper, German Kämpfer, Danish kæmper. Compare also English kemp (“knight, warrior”), from Middle English kempe (“kemper, warrior”), from Old English cempa (“warrior, soldier”).

senses: Methylated spirits.
examples: Ben Cropp, aided by his wife Lynn, tests the effectiveness of metho and vinegar against box jellyfish stings (above); see Ben′s foreword for details of the experiment.

Assist students to design and construct models of hot-air balloons ranging from those using shopping bags and hair dryers, to those using tissue paper and metho burners, depending on the resources available.

senses: Circular; going round.
ety: From French circulatoire, from Latin circulatorius.

senses: To ban, remove or reduce the numbers of nuclear weapons in an area.
A Japanese confection consisting of two sponge cake patties baked to resemble gongs, sandwiching a filling of sweet azuki bean paste.
ety: From Japanese 銅鑼焼(どらや)き (dorayaki).

senses: A person who adheres to the literal representation of a statement or law.
A person who translates a text literally.
One who works in the style of literalism.
A talking drum of West Africa.
A bag in which nuts are carried or stored.
Across the Pennines
A municipality in various Latin American countries.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish municipio. Doublet of municipium.

senses: To make or become gross (all senses).
examples: She could tell he assessed her again then, and saw how she had grossened, and wondered why he'd bothered coming weeks before to her door, asking for her company.

senses: Of a number, expressed in hexadecimal.
ety: 1952, from hexa- + decimal; see the Wikipedia article for more information. Piecewise doublet of sexadecimal.

senses: Having a diet that consists mostly of fruit; fruit-eating.
examples: Although the vampire bat is known for feeding on blood, most species of bat eat insects, and many are frugivorous.

senses: A musical instrument made of blown-glass bowls mounted on a spindle turned originally by a foot pedal, and played with wetted fingers, producing an ethereal sound. Technically, it is a crystallophone.
ety: Coined by Benjamin Franklin, its inventor; built on Italian armonia (“harmony”). Glass harmonica is a corruption of Franklin's original word, a back-formation influenced by harmonica (a reed instrument invented sixty years later).
